title: Minimum Common Value in Two Sorted Arrays
description:
# Minimum Common Value in Two Sorted Arrays

Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, each sorted in nondecreasing order, return the smallest integer that appears in both arrays.

If the arrays have no common value, return `-1`. Duplicate values may appear in either array, but the answer is a value, not a count or an index. Either array may be empty.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums1 = [1,2,3], nums2 = [2,4]

**Output:** 2

**Explanation:** The value `2` appears in both arrays and is the smallest common value.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums1 = [1,2,3,6], nums2 = [2,3,4,5]

**Output:** 2

**Explanation:** Both `2` and `3` are common values, so the smallest one is `2`.

## Constraints:

* `0 <= nums1.length, nums2.length <= 10^5`
* `-10^9 <= nums1[i], nums2[i] <= 10^9`
* Both arrays are sorted in nondecreasing order.

solutions.name: Merge-Style Two Pointers
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use one pointer for each sorted array. If the two current values are equal, return that value. Otherwise, advance the pointer that points to the smaller value, because that smaller value can no longer match any future value in the other sorted array.

## Key Insight

The arrays are scanned from small to large. Therefore the first equality encountered is automatically the smallest common value, and no later value can be a better answer.

## Complexity Analysis

Each pointer only moves forward, so the time complexity is O(n + m), where `n` and `m` are the array lengths. The algorithm uses O(1) extra space.

solutions.name: Duplicate-Block Skipping
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same sorted merge idea, but when one side is smaller, skip the whole block of that repeated value instead of moving by only one index. If the current values are equal, return immediately.

## Key Insight

For nondecreasing arrays, repeated copies of a value are adjacent. When `nums1[i] < nums2[j]`, every copy of `nums1[i]` is still too small to match `nums2[j]` or any later value, so the entire block can be discarded at once.

## Complexity Analysis

Every element belongs to one skipped block, so the total time complexity remains O(n + m). The algorithm uses O(1) extra space.

solutions.name: Hash Set Lookup
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert every value from `nums1` into a hash set. Then scan `nums2` from left to right and return the first value that appears in the set.

## Key Insight

Even though this route does not use both sorted arrays symmetrically, scanning `nums2` in sorted order still guarantees that the first hit is the smallest common value. It trades memory for a simpler membership test.

## Complexity Analysis

Building the set and scanning the second array take O(n + m) expected time. The set may store O(n) distinct values.

solutions.name: Binary Search Shorter Candidates
solutions.description:
## Approach

Choose the shorter array as the candidate list. Iterate through that array in sorted order and binary-search each candidate in the longer array. The first candidate found in both arrays is returned.

## Key Insight

The candidate array is sorted, so the first successful candidate is the smallest common value. Searching the longer array keeps the number of binary searches as small as possible.

## Complexity Analysis

If the shorter array has length `s` and the longer one has length `l`, the time complexity is O(s * log l). The algorithm uses O(1) extra space.

solutions.name: Alternating Lower-Bound Jumps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep one index in each array. When the current values differ, jump the smaller side forward with a lower-bound search to the first position whose value is at least the larger side's current value. Repeat until the values match or one array ends.

## Key Insight

A lower-bound jump is a binary-search version of advancing the smaller pointer. It is especially clear when the arrays have large gaps: all values below the other side's current value are impossible matches and can be skipped as a group.

## Complexity Analysis

Each jump moves one index forward, and each jump costs logarithmic time in the target array. The worst-case time complexity is O((n + m) * log(n + m)), and the algorithm uses O(1) extra space.
